sections.title: Time expressions
sections.content:
Time expressions that refer to the present, such as this morning / week / month and today, can be used with either past simple or present perfect verbs.
If we think of this morning (etc.) as a past, completed time period, then we use the past simple; if we think of this morning (etc.) as a time period which includes the present moment, then we use the present perfect. Compare:
• I didn't shave this morning. (= the morning is over and I didn't shave) and
• I haven't shaved this morning. (= it is still the morning and I might shave later)

sections.title: Time clauses with since
sections.content:
In a sentence which includes a time clause with since, we generally prefer a past simple verb in the time clause (referring to a particular point in the past) and a present perfect verb in the main clause:
• Since Mr Dodson became president unemployment has increased. (rather than ... has become ...)
• She hasn't been able to play tennis since she broke her arm. (rather than ... has broken ...)
Note, however, that we use the present perfect in the time clause with since if the two situations described in the main clause and time clause extend until the present:
• Have you met any of your neighbours since you've lived here? (not ... you lived ...)

sections.title: Present perfect for future events
sections.content:
With time clauses introduced by after, when, until, as soon as, once, by the time and the time expressions the minute / second / moment the past simple refers to past, completed events and the present perfect refers to future events. Compare these examples:
• After she left hospital (past), she had a long holiday. and
• After Lucas has left school (future), he will be spending six months in India.
• The minute I got the news about Anna (past) I telephoned my parents. and
• I'll contact you the minute I've got my exam results. (future)
In the time clause in sentences like this it is possible to use the past perfect instead of the past simple (e.g. After she had left ...) and the present simple instead of the present perfect (e.g. After Lucas leaves ...) with the same meaning (see also Unit 5).

sections.title: News reports
sections.content:
In news reports, you will often read about or hear recent events introduced with the present perfect, and then the past simple or other past tenses are used to give details:
• A Russian spacecraft has returned safely to Earth with its two passengers. US astronaut Scott Keane and Russian cosmonaut Olga Kaleri landed in the early hours of Wednesday.
• An American woman has become the first person to make 2 million contributions to Dictionary File. Esther Miller began editing the site eight years ago.

sections.title: It is the first time...
sections.content:
After the pattern It / This / That is / will be the first time ... we generally use the present perfect in the next clause:
•
That's the first time
I've seen Jan look embarrassed. (reporting a past event)
•
It won't be the first time
she has voted against the government. (talking about a future event)
Note that after It / This / That was the first time ... we generally use the past perfect (see Unit 5):
•
It was the first time
I'd talked to Dimitra outside the office.

exercises.question: A: Shall I make us some dinner? ... B: No, thanks. I ___ to the dentist this afternoon and my mouth hurts too much to eat anything. (go)
exercises.hint: The period of the afternoon is fully completed in the speaker's mind.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: went
The period of the afternoon is fully completed in the speaker's mind.

exercises.question: I ___ three lectures today and I still have two more later this afternoon.
exercises.hint: The period 'today' includes the present moment, and more lectures are expected.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have had
The period 'today' includes the present moment, and more lectures are expected.

exercises.question: It was so hot today that I ___ shorts and a T-shirt at work. (wear)
exercises.hint: The work day is over, even though it's still 'today'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: wore
The work day is over, even though it's still 'today'.

exercises.question: We ___ £400 on food this month and there's another week to go before I get paid. (spend)
exercises.hint: The period 'this month' is incomplete.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have spent
Use the present perfect when the time period described is not yet complete. Expressions like this week, this year, today (when the day is still ongoing), and so far all signal an incomplete period — and an incomplete period requires the present perfect.

exercises.question: A: Do you want a lift home? B: No, I ___ this morning because my alarm clock didn't go off, so I need to work late. (oversleep)
exercises.hint: The 'morning' is definitely over as they are leaving work now.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: overslept
The 'morning' is definitely over as they are leaving work now.

exercises.question: I ___ much of the report yet, but I have to finish it by the weekend. (read - negative)
exercises.hint: The period before the deadline is incomplete ('yet').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: haven't read
The period before the deadline is incomplete ('yet').

exercises.question: Maria ___ to go swimming since she ___ in the river. (not want / fall)
exercises.hint: Use past simple in the time clause (point in past) and present perfect in main clause.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: hasn't wanted / fell
Use past simple in the time clause (point in past) and present perfect in main clause. The present perfect connects past events to the present moment — used for recent events, life experience, or ongoing results.

exercises.question: Since she ___ at the company she ___ a day off through illness.
exercises.hint: Point in past vs state continuing to present.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: worked / hasn't had
Point in past vs state continuing to present.

exercises.question: Since he ___ from a house fire, he ___ on TV almost every day.
exercises.hint: Past simple for the single event, present perfect for the recurring events since.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was rescued / has been
Since introduces a point in the past and requires the present perfect (or perfect continuous) in the main clause. The action or state started at that past point and continues to — or still has relevance at — the present moment.

exercises.question: A lot ___ since I last ___ to you.
exercises.hint: Main clause: events continuing to now. Time clause: point in past.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has happened / spoke
Main clause: events continuing to now. Time clause: point in past. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Since I ___ to drive I ___ much more independent. (be able / feel)
exercises.hint: Both situations extend until the present.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been able / have felt
Both situations extend until the present. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Stefan's reading ___ enormously since he ___ at school.
exercises.hint: Past state in the time clause vs continuing effect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has improved / was
Past state in the time clause vs continuing effect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Remember that after you signed the contract you won't be able to change your mind.
exercises.hint: Present perfect referring to a future event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Change to 'have signed'
Present perfect referring to a future event. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Carlo's injury only became apparent after he signed to play for United.
exercises.hint: Past simple refers to past, completed events.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Sentence is correct as is
Past simple refers to past, completed events.

exercises.question: As soon as I finished college I want to travel around Australia.
acceptable: Both 'have finished' and 'finish' are correct replacements
exercises.hint: Both present and present perfect can refer to future events in time clauses.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both 'have finished' and 'finish' are correct replacements
Both present and present perfect can refer to future events in time clauses. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: I didn't have time to check the essay. I handed it in as soon as I finished it.
exercises.hint: Past simple for a completed action.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Sentence is correct as is
Past simple for a completed action.

exercises.question: I'll probably have finished breakfast by the time the children got up.
acceptable: Both 'get up' and 'have got up' are correct replacements
exercises.hint: Referring to a future event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both 'get up' and 'have got up' are correct replacements
Referring to a future event. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: When President Ismail ___ in Paris this evening, it will be the first time she ___ Europe since her election victory in May. (arrive, visit)
exercises.hint: Present simple for future condition, present perfect after 'the first time'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: arrives / has visited
After it is the first/second/only time, use the present perfect in the following clause. The present perfect connects the current moment to all previous occasions — making it the natural choice for expressing "first time" statements.

exercises.question: The Victoria Hospital ___ to new patients after more cases of food poisoning. Three patients ___ last week in the outbreak. (close, die)
exercises.hint: News introduction vs exact past details.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has closed / died
News reports and announcements use the present perfect to introduce a recent event with current relevance. The exact time is less important than the fact that the event has just happened and affects the present situation. After the first mention, the past simple is used for the details.

exercises.question: The rate of inflation ___ to 4.8%. It's the first time in nearly two years that the rate ___ below 5%. (drop, fall)
exercises.hint: Introducing news + present perfect after 'the first time'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has dropped / has fallen
News reports and announcements use the present perfect to introduce a recent event with current relevance. The exact time is less important than the fact that the event has just happened and affects the present situation. After the first mention, the past simple is used for the details.

exercises.question: Nearly 600 laptops ___ from Ministry of Defence staff over the past five years. However, a spokesperson ___ that there had been no security problems as none of the computers ___ secret information. (steal, insist, hold)
options: were stolen / has insisted / has held
exercises.hint: Recent news overview (passive present perfect) followed by past details.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been stolen / insisted / held
News reports and announcements use the present perfect to introduce a recent event with current relevance. The exact time is less important than the fact that the event has just happened and affects the present situation. After the first mention, the past simple is used for the details.

exercises.question: I ___ (visit) Paris three times in my life.
exercises.hint: Life experience up to now, no specific time → present perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have visited
The present perfect is used for life experience when no specific past time is mentioned. The focus is on the experience itself, not when it happened.

exercises.question: She ___ (finish) the report an hour ago.
exercises.hint: Specific completed time in the past ('an hour ago') → past simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: finished
'An hour ago' is a specific past time reference. Whenever a specific past time is given or implied, use the past simple, not the present perfect.

exercises.question: ___ (you / ever / eat) sushi? It's delicious!
exercises.hint: 'Ever' asking about life experience up to now → present perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Have you ever eaten
'Ever' in questions about experience up to the present moment signals the present perfect. The question is about any point in your life, not a specific time.

exercises.question: I ___ (not / see) Tom since last Tuesday.
exercises.hint: 'Since' + a past point → present perfect for the gap continuing to now.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: haven't seen
'Since' always requires the present perfect when describing a state or action that has continued from a past point up to now.
